profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for a 6-week internal pilot on Team Atlas, a Scrum-based product team building a customer onboarding workflow. The company wants to test whether short perception surveys about agile practices can be paired with software development artifacts to detect behaviors such as test-first work, review discipline, and sprint collaboration before rolling the approach out to other teams. The agenda is to define the pilot timeline, decide what development data will be collected, agree what the first report should look like, and assign implementation responsibilities. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the baseline period, the data pipeline, the survey cadence, and the format of the pilot readout for engineering leadership and the team retrospective.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Scrum team operations, delivery planning, engineering coaching, team health
members.background: Elena was previously a Scrum Master and now manages a cross-functional application team; she is sponsoring the pilot because she wants evidence about which agile practices are actually being used rather than relying only on retrospective impressions.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to feel safe and lightweight so the team will participate honestly, and she is especially concerned that any reporting not be seen as individual performance monitoring or as a hidden expansion of scope beyond what the team expects.
hidden_assumptions: The 'baseline sprint' is the upcoming Sprint 18, because it is the last sprint before she starts structured coaching changes the following Monday.
'Development data' for this pilot means only Team Atlas's own GitHub repos, pull requests, and CI runs, since those are the artifacts she believes the team already accepts as fair game.
A 'team-level report' excludes any contributor-by-contributor visualization, even if names are removed, because anonymity alone does not make a report feel non-evaluative.
A 'role breakdown' refers to Scrum roles for the sprint roster—Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers—because that is the role framing used in the research she has in mind.

members.name: Marcus Chen
members.expertise: Engineering telemetry, analytics pipelines, repository mining, internal dashboards
members.background: Marcus supports multiple engineering teams by turning software delivery exhaust data into reusable metrics and dashboards; he has built prior pipelines combining GitHub, Jira, and CI data for process-improvement work.
members.private_state: He wants to build the pilot on top of existing warehouse tables so the work scales to other teams later, and he worries that a too-thin dataset will make the results inconclusive or force manual cleanup.
hidden_assumptions: The 'baseline sprint' is the most recently completed sprint, because a baseline should already exist before any new instrumentation or reporting begins.

'Development data' naturally includes Jira state transitions and activity in shared platform repos touched by Team Atlas, since those are standard engineering artifacts already available in the warehouse.
A 'team-level report' can still contain pseudonymous contributor timelines or row-level traces as long as the presentation is for internal process learning rather than external performance review.
A 'role breakdown' should use the company directory and warehouse job-role fields, because those labels are stable, queryable, and close enough to how work responsibilities are distributed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the baseline sprint
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to collect a 'baseline sprint' before the pilot readout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means Sprint 18, the upcoming sprint that occurs before her coaching adjustments begin, so it is the last untouched observation window.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means Sprint 17, the most recently completed sprint, because a baseline should precede the pilot setup and be immediately queryable from existing data.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'baseline before the pilot' sounds precise enough on its own, and both options seem reasonable in a planning conversation, so neither person feels a need to restate the sprint number explicitly.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in development data
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will use 'development data' or 'engineering artifacts' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means Team Atlas's owned GitHub repositories, pull requests, and CI/test runs only, excluding Jira workflow data and excluding shared services maintained by another team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the standard telemetry bundle: GitHub activity, CI runs, Jira ticket transitions, and relevant pull requests in shared services such as the auth-service repo when Atlas developers contributed there.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: 'Development data' is a familiar umbrella term, and both participants believe they are talking about routine artifacts rather than making a controversial data-source decision, so they never enumerate the boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a team-level report
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the first deliverable should be a 'team-level report.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means only aggregate charts and summaries at whole-team or Scrum-role level, with no contributor-specific timelines or distributions shown anywhere in the deck or dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the report is team-level if the headline conclusions are about the team, even if supporting views include pseudonymous contributor traces to explain variance within the team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely trying to avoid overt individual evaluation, so the phrase 'team-level' creates false consensus even though their thresholds for acceptable granularity differ.

misalignment_points.topic: Which roles are used in the role breakdown
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to doing a 'role breakdown' because the study is about how role affects perceptions of agile practice.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the actual Scrum roles assigned on Team Atlas during the sprint: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the warehouse role fields from the company directory: engineering manager, frontend engineer, backend engineer, QA engineer, and product manager.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The single word 'role' feels unambiguous in everyday software work, and both candidate categorizations are common enough that neither person anticipates a mismatch.
